niche_preference_profile: This user prefers interfaces that feel clear, complete, and easy to scan: airy but not empty, with strong visual hierarchy, obvious headings and controls, well-separated sections/cards, high contrast, and enough content density to feel finished and useful. They like direct, specific labels and task-oriented copy, and they respond well to prominent primary actions and visible affordances. They generally prefer polished, modern layouts with restrained clutter, though they sometimes favor richer visual treatment when it improves warmth or completeness.

criteria.description: Strong separation between sections, clear focal points, and obvious emphasis on titles, controls, and primary actions.
Bold, readable headings and labels with strong text contrast and minimal washed-out secondary text.
Content should be broken into clearly separated sections or cards rather than blended into one continuous panel.
Toggles, buttons, and row actions should look actionable and be easy to notice at a glance.
Surfaces, text, and background should have enough contrast to improve clarity and perceived polish.
Layouts should feel spacious and breathable, but still populated enough to avoid looking sparse or unfinished.
The screen should feel fully populated and production-ready, not blank, placeholder-like, or awkwardly underfilled.
Labels, titles, and helper text should be explicit, specific, and operational rather than vague or overly conversational.
A single primary action should be visually obvious and easy to find, with strong emphasis over secondary actions.
Search fields and labels should clearly indicate what can be found or managed, using concrete terms like names, numbers, or status.
List items should have clear row boundaries, metadata, and inline actions so each entry feels usable and self-explanatory.
The interface should feel modern, app-like, and refined rather than dated, generic, or overly utilitarian.
Navigation chrome, extra labels, arrows, and banners should be kept restrained so they do not compete with the main task.
Section titles and category labels should be familiar, direct, and clearly tied to the user’s task.
Screens should include the actions needed to complete the task, not just browse or search; management flows should feel actionable.
